cim: Utah tests if AI can safely diagnose patients, prescribe medication
cim_eredeti: Utah tests if AI can safely diagnose patients, prescribe medication
szoveg_eredeti:
SALT LAKE CITY (KUTV) — Utah is running a first-of-its-kind experiment to test whether artificial intelligence, or AI, can safely deliver health care, including diagnosing patients and prescribing medication without a patient seeing a doctor.

Utah's Office of AI Policy is overseeing pilot programs with seven companies testing different applications of AI in health care.

One of those companies is Nolla Health, which operates the Nolla Derm app. It allows patients to receive an acne diagnosis and prescription without ever seeing a doctor face-to-face.

Patients who are older than 18 and not pregnant can download the app, pay a subscription fee and upload five pictures of their acne. The AI system, which has been previously trained, then makes a diagnosis and recommends treatment.

Dr. Zaid Fadul, chief medical adviser for Nolla Health, said the AI can prescribe only from a list of five to eight approved generic medications commonly used to treat acne. The app prescribes Nolla Derm creams, not oral medications.

"The AI is not prescribing things out of left field," Fadul said.

During the first phase of the pilot, Fadul and a second physician must review and approve every prescription before it goes to a patient. If the AI performs well in the first stage, the program can advance to later stages, giving the technology more autonomy.

Fadul said acne medication is relatively low-risk, making it a good way to test AI's ability to prescribe treatment for patients who often have difficulty getting a timely appointment with a dermatologist.

"You shouldn't have to wait three months to get into a dermatologist to ask if you can get benzoyl peroxide. That's not necessary," he said.

At a time when there is a shortage of doctors and residents in some communities, especially rural areas, have limited access to physicians and specialists, AI could help improve access to care, Fadul said.

"I'm a big champion of telehealth and now integrating AI — not because I want to replace physicians. I want to increase access to those physicians," he added.

Utah's Office of AI Policy said the pilot programs will go through three stages and can operate for a maximum of three years.

Independent evaluators selected by the state, but paid by the participating companies, will determine whether the technology is safe and appropriate before allowing it to advance to the next stage.

Zach Boyd, director of the Utah Office of AI Policy, said Utah does not have enough doctors and other health care professionals to meet the growing demand for care.

The goal is to determine whether AI can take on some routine clinical tasks, allowing physicians to focus their time and attention on more complex medical issues, such as cancer.

"We are all suffering with the way the health care system is right now. So, to have a realistic possibility to expand the care available to people is such a big deal to me," he said.

Boyd does not believe AI will replace doctors anytime soon.

"There is so much demand for health care right now. I don't think there's any universe where we are going to put doctors out of jobs anytime soon," he said.

Boyd acknowledged that AI will make mistakes, just as human health care providers do. But he said the technology will have to demonstrate that it can perform at least as well as a human provider before the state allows it to advance.

If the pilot programs are successful, their results could help guide the state in making regulatory changes, as Utah law only allows humans to practice medicine.

Current laws governing patient safety and privacy apply to all the pilot programs.

Michelle McOmber, president of the Utah Medical Association, which represents most doctors in the state, questions whether AI should be placed between doctors and patients.

"We don't think it's appropriate to take the physician out of the loop of health care in prescribing a medication. How does that help the patient?" she said.

McOmber said AI could be useful in helping doctors with paperwork and other time-consuming administrative tasks, freeing them to spend more time with patients.

She said treating patients involves much more than determining which medication they need. Physicians also need face-to-face time to evaluate a patient's mental health, listen to their concerns and consider other factors that AI may not adequately address.

"AI is not the answer to all the problems with health care," she said.
